questions.q: What problem is Salesforce DX (SFDX) built to solve?
options: Replacing the need for a production org entirely
Supporting source-driven development — treating a Git repository, not the org, as the source of truth
Removing the need for any code review
Automatically writing Apex test classes
questions.explain: SFDX provides the project structure, CLI, and source-format metadata representation that make treating a Git repo as the source of truth (with orgs as deployment targets) practical.

questions.q: Why does Salesforce DX's source format work better with Git than the older metadata API format?
options: Source format doesn't use XML at all
Source format stores everything in a single compressed file
Source format breaks metadata into small, individually readable files, producing smaller, cleaner diffs and merges
Metadata API format cannot be committed to Git at all
questions.explain: Source format splits metadata into granular, one-concept-per-file units (like a single field's own file), so a small change shows up as a small, readable diff rather than noise inside one large bundled file.

options: A permanent production org used only for testing
A backup copy of the Git repository stored on Salesforce's servers
A special branch name reserved for release candidates
A temporary, disposable org created on demand from a tracked definition file
questions.explain: A scratch org is created fresh from a project-scratch-def.json file committed to the repo, used for a feature's testing, and discarded once the work is done — no manual sandbox cleanup required.

questions.q: Which command retrieves metadata changes from an org into the local source-format project folder?
options: sf project retrieve start
sf project deploy start
git commit
git merge
questions.explain: sf project retrieve start pulls metadata from the target org into the local project; sf project deploy start does the reverse, pushing local metadata to a target org.

questions.q: In the retrieve-commit-deploy cycle described in this lesson, what is the purpose of running git status / git diff after retrieving metadata?
options: To automatically deploy the change to production
To delete the scratch org
To review exactly which metadata files changed, catching any accidental unrelated change pulled in alongside the intended one
To generate a package.xml automatically
questions.explain: Reviewing the diff after a retrieve is how a developer catches metadata that got pulled in unintentionally alongside the intended change, before it's committed and pushed.
